## Design

### 2026-10-22 – The 11-Hour Master Grind - From Schematic to Production-Ready MIDI Controller PCB

**10h**

The 11-Hour Master Grind - From Schematic to Production-Ready MIDI Controller PCB

Today was an absolute marathon. What started as an idea for a custom, screenless geometric touch MIDI controller turned into a full 11-hour hardware design session. I took this project from a blank canvas all the way through schematic mapping, custom touch-pad geometry creation, board layout, artistic Edge.Cuts profiling, and finally generating the complete Gerber package.

Phase 1: Schematic Design and Control Architecture
Before dropping a single copper trace, I had to map out the electrical logic for a complex hybrid instrument. I integrated the ESP32-S3 module to handle fast processing, capacitive touch inputs, and USB/BLE MIDI communication. For controls and inputs, I wired up 4 slide potentiometers, rotary encoders with built-in push switches, and tactile navigation buttons. I added auxiliary ICs like the ADS1115 ADC and PCF8574 I/O expander to multiply available analog and digital pins. Finally, I designated specific touch-capable GPIO nets for 7 individual piano keys and 4 circular drum pads.

Phase 2: Custom Footprint Creation and Touch Surface Physics
Standard rectangular pads were not going to cut it for a real musical interface, so I had to dive deep into custom footprint editing. I built custom geometric polygons for interlocking L-shaped and T-shaped white and black keys. To tame the pad editor, I learned that standard graphic merges leave tiny anchor points, so the fix was jumping straight into Pad Edit Mode to draw custom primitive polygons directly inside the pad definition. This ensured the entire physical shape functions as a unified electrical node. I checked and enabled F.Mask clearances across all touch surfaces to strip away the solder mask, leaving raw copper exposed so finger contact registers instantly, and spaced everything out with clean clearance gaps to prevent cross-talk.

Phase 3: Component Placement and Ergonomic Layout
With the footprints built, I updated the PCB layout and organized the components into 3 intuitive ergonomic zones. The top deck housed the ESP32-S3 module, sliders, encoders, and tactile push switches for real-time parameter control. The middle zone featured 4 large, perfectly spaced circular capacitive drum pads for finger drumming. The bottom bed contained a custom 7-key piano keybed array designed for natural hand-playing.

Phase 4: Sculpting the Edge.Cuts and Backside Art
Instead of a boring rectangle, the board needed a physical profile that matched its purpose. I switched to the Edge.Cuts layer and used graphic lines and arcs to trace a custom silhouette around the entire assembly, leaving a safe 2mm to 3mm margin from the copper traces. For personal branding, I used KiCad's Bitmap to Component Converter to turn custom artwork and logos into footprints, then flipped them onto the bottom layers for silkscreen and exposed copper art. Finally, I fired up the 3D Viewer to inspect the final physical shape and make sure everything looked clean and professional.

Phase 5: Routing and Exporting Manufacturing Gerbers
With the layout locked in, I routed clean signal traces from the ESP32 and expansion ICs down to all control terminals and touch pads. I went to the fabrication outputs for Gerbers, making sure essential layers like front copper, back copper, masks, silkscreens, and Edge.Cuts were fully captured. I generated standard drill and slot files for mounting holes and encoder pins, and then compressed all output files into a clean archive ready to drop straight into a manufacturer's online 3D viewer.

Next Session: Firmware Development
With the hardware fully engineered and packed into a production-ready Gerber archive, the physical board is officially done. In the next session, I will be moving on to software: writing the firmware to handle ESP32 capacitive touch thresholds, mapping inputs to MIDI messages, and setting up the USB and BLE-MIDI stack.

Total Time Spent: 10.0hours.
